source.name: Turkish Pop
source.lineage: Türk pop müziği, running from the 1960s aranjman craze of foreign melodies with Turkish lyrics through Sezen Aksu's songwriting school and the 1990s Tarkan-era boom — 95-130 BPM verse-chorus songs with darbuka and programmed kit under Western pop harmony, bağlama or kanun countermelodies, synth pads and horn stabs, and a melismatic, makam-inflected but tempered lead vocal.

extras.description: Turkish pop began as aranjman — imported French and Italian melodies refitted with Turkish lyrics in the 1960s — and became a self-sustaining songwriting industry through Sezen Aksu, whose circle wrote much of the canon that Tarkan, Sertab Erener, and Hande Yener later carried to Europe. The records marry Western pop harmony and 1990s dance production to Anatolian melodic contour and to a percussion bed where darbuka and bendir sit beside the drum machine, with vocals ornamented in makam style even over tempered accompaniment. It is distinguished from arabesk by its cosmopolitan, non-fatalistic register and lighter orchestration, and from Anadolu rock by foregrounding the singer and the dance groove rather than the electric guitar.

extras.description: Art punk emerged in 1976-79 among art-school-trained musicians who took punk's rejection of virtuosity as license for formal experiment rather than speed. source.name: Cambodian Rock (Phnom Penh Psych)
source.lineage: Phnom Penh popular music of roughly 1963-1975, made by Sinn Sisamouth, Ros Serey Sothea, Pen Ran and Yol Aularong for radio and nightclub, grafting surf-reverb and fuzz guitar, combo organ, Farfisa-and-saxophone bandstand arrangements and a-go-go or slow-rock backbeats onto Khmer ramvong and romvong dance rhythms, with high, nasal, heavily ornamented Khmer vocal delivery on top.

extras.description: Cambodian rock formed when American Forces radio and French yé-yé records reached Phnom Penh nightclubs, and it kept Khmer melodic ornament and vocal placement intact while borrowing wholesale from surf, garage and soul instrumentation. Recordings are dry-to-slapback, often small-room and lightly overdubbed, with organ and reverbed guitar sharing the top and horns arranged in unison stabs. What separates it from Thai string and Vietnamese kích động nhạc of the same years is the vocal line: intensely melismatic, high-set, and phrased against the beat rather than with it. The scene ended abruptly in 1975, and most of its principals were killed.

source.name: Ostrock (GDR rock)
source.lineage: East German rock produced from the late 1960s to 1990 under the state Amiga label and the mandatory 60-percent domestic-repertoire rule, with Puhdys, City, Karat, Silly and Pankow writing German-language songs that fold Anglo hard-rock riffing and progressive keyboard arrangements into radio-length forms, using Hammond and string-machine pads, folk violin colour, restrained heavy-rock guitar and lyrics coded to slip past censors.

extras.description: Ostrock is the rock repertoire made inside the GDR between the late 1960s and reunification, shaped as much by Amiga's monopoly, state licensing of musicians and airplay quotas as by musical choice. The result is a well-drilled, conservatively engineered hard rock with prominent organ and string-machine, competent but unshowy guitar solos, and German lyrics whose ambiguity was the point — City's Am Fenster and Karat's Über sieben Brücken became standards on both sides of the border. It is distinguished from West German Deutschrock by its state-studio uniformity and metaphorical lyricism, and from Soviet magnitizdat rock by being officially released rather than clandestinely taped.

extras.description: The Dunedin sound was made in a small South Island university town in the early 1980s, where isolation and the Flying Nun label's tiny budgets produced records cut to four-track in flats and halls. Its markers are jangling, thin, treble-forward guitar, Velvet Underground-derived drone and repetition, unpolished tape hiss, and flat undramatic vocals sitting low in the mix. It is more rhythmically insistent and less twee than UK C86 jangle, and far rawer in fidelity than the studio-made Paisley Underground.

extras.description: Indie rock names the guitar-band music that circulated through independent distribution networks and college radio in the United States and Britain from the early 1980s, defined as much by its economics and recording budgets as by any single sound. It is distinguished from mainstream alternative rock by production scale and refusal of vocal polish, and from punk by wider harmonic and dynamic range and slower average tempos.
